title: Parents Maintenance Act Bangladesh: NRB & Child Duties
metaDescription: Learn legal duties of children and NRBs under the Parents Maintenance Act 2013 (Pita-Matar Bhoron-Poshon Ain) in Bangladesh, penalties, and filing steps.
keywords: NRB duty to maintain parents Bangladesh
heroIntro: Under Sections 3 and 4 of the Parents Maintenance Act, 2013 (Pita-Matar Bhoron-Poshon Ain, 2013), every adult child—including Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) living abroad—is legally obligated to provide reasonable food, shelter, healthcare, and regular companionship or communication to elderly parents. Wilful neglect carries a criminal penalty of up to BDT 1,00,000 fine or three months' imprisonment.

quickAnswer.heading: At a Glance: Parents Maintenance Act, 2013
points: Primary Statute: Pita-Matar Bhoron-Poshon Ain, 2013 (Parents Maintenance Act, 2013), Sections 3–8.
Who Is Protected: Biological father and mother (including in old-age homes if neglected).
Penalty for Neglect: Fine up to BDT 1,00,000; in default, simple imprisonment up to 3 months (Section 5).
Competent Court: First-Class Judicial Magistrate or Metropolitan Magistrate Court (Section 7).

sections.h2: Statutory Duty Under the Parents Maintenance Act, 2013
sections.content:
Section 3 of the Parents Maintenance Act, 2013 mandates that every child must ensure the maintenance of their parents, and if there is more than one child, they must mutually share the responsibility. 'Maintenance' under Section 2(b) explicitly encompasses food, clothing, medical treatment, residential accommodation, and reasonable personal care.

Under Section 3(3)–(5), no child may force a parent to live in an old-age home against their will, and children living separately must maintain regular contact and provide reasonable monthly financial support. Importantly, Section 4 extends a secondary duty to maternal and paternal grandparents if the parents are absent or unable to maintain them.

This law operates independently of property inheritance; children cannot refuse maintenance on the ground that the father has not transferred land—see our guide on children's property claims while a father is alive and inheritance rights in Bangladesh.

sections.h2: How the Law Applies to NRB Children Living Abroad
sections.content:
Living in the UK, USA, Canada, or UAE does not exempt an NRB from statutory maintenance duties toward parents residing in Bangladesh. When one sibling lives abroad while another cares for ageing parents in Dhaka, disputes frequently arise over unequal financial contribution or alleged neglect.

Under Section 7 of the Act, a parent can file a complaint before the local Magistrate Court, and the court may refer the matter to the Union Parishad Chairman, City Corporation Ward Councillor, or an appointed mediator for amicable settlement under Section 8. For NRB children, sending monthly remittances through official banking channels—with clear bank receipts—provides verifiable proof of compliance and prevents false criminal allegations. For cross-border support, see our NRB Legal Help Desk and legal remittance rules.

sections.h2: Penalties and Criminal Liability Under Section 5
sections.content:
Section 5 of the Parents Maintenance Act, 2013 makes wilful failure to maintain parents, or forcing them into an old-age home without consent, a criminal offence punishable by a fine up to BDT 1,00,000, and in default of payment, simple imprisonment up to three (3) months. Furthermore, Section 6 penalises anyone (including a spouse or in-law) who abets or obstructs a child from maintaining their parents with the same penalty.

Offence / DutyStatutory SectionPenalty / Outcome
Failure to provide food, shelter & healthcareSection 3 & Section 5Fine up to BDT 1,00,000; default 3 months' imprisonment.
Abetting or obstructing maintenanceSection 6Same penalty as principal offender (up to BDT 1,00,000 fine).
Mediation & SettlementSection 8Court may refer to Union Parishad / Ward Councillor for compromise.

Because offences under the Act are bailable and compoundable (Section 7), an accused child facing summons or warrant can apply for bail or settle amicably; review our bail guide in Bangladesh or consult a criminal lawyer in Dhaka.

sections.h2: Step-by-Step Procedure to File a Maintenance Complaint
sections.content:
An aggrieved father or mother may initiate proceedings before the Magistrate Court with minimal formality under Section 7 of the 2013 Act.

  1. Send a Written Notice or Family Mediation Request: Before approaching court, send a written notice or engage respected elders / Ward Councillor to record the refusal of support.
  2. Draft a Formal Complaint (CR Case): Prepare a written petition before the Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) detailing the child's income, residence, and refusal to maintain.
  3. Attach Identity & Medical Proof: Enclose NID copies, birth/family records proving parentage, and medical bills or living expense estimates.
  4. Magistrate Cognisance & Summons: Under Section 7, the Magistrate examines the complainant on oath and issues summons (or refers the matter to mediation under Section 8).
  5. Enforce Monthly Maintenance or Compromise: On compromise or order, monthly support is paid via bank transfer or chamber deposit; consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam for representation in Dhaka courts.

sections.h2: Documents Checklist for Parents & NRB Respondents
sections.content:
Whether you are a parent seeking statutory support or an NRB child defending against an unfair complaint, assemble these core records.

  • National ID (NID) cards and passport copies establishing the parent-child relationship.
  • Medical prescriptions, hospital bills, utility receipts, and rent or living expense statements.
  • Bank remittance slips, bKash/Nagad statements, or wire transfer receipts proving prior financial support (essential for NRBs).
  • Copy of any registered Heba gift deed or family property arrangement if property transfer was linked to care promises.
  • Written legal notice or Union Parishad / Ward Councillor mediation minutes, if conducted.

For related family matters, read our guide on child custody for NRBs or book a free initial consultation with our Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court chamber.

faqs.question: Are married daughters also legally responsible for maintaining their parents in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Section 3 of the Parents Maintenance Act, 2013 uses the gender-neutral term 'sontan' (child), meaning both sons and daughters—whether married or unmarried—share the legal duty to maintain their parents according to their financial capacity.

faqs.question: Can a father or mother take back gifted property if a child stops maintaining them?
faqs.answer: Under the Parents Maintenance Act, 2013, the court imposes a fine or orders maintenance rather than automatically cancelling a registered deed. However, if a Heba or gift deed contained an express written condition of lifetime maintenance, a civil suit for revocation may be examined under the Specific Relief Act, 1877.

faqs.question: What if an NRB child sends money to one sibling in Dhaka who fails to give it to the parents?
faqs.answer: To protect themselves from liability under Section 5, NRB children should transfer maintenance directly to the parent's own bank account or mobile financial wallet rather than through an intermediary sibling, and retain official wire receipts.

faqs.question: Is an offence under the Parents Maintenance Act, 2013 bailable?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Section 7 of the Act, offences are cognisable, bailable, and compoundable. This means the accused child is entitled to seek bail as a matter of right and can resolve the dispute through a court-approved compromise at any stage.

faqs.question: Can a parent file a case even if the child lives permanently in the UK or USA?
faqs.answer: Yes, a parent residing in Bangladesh can file a complaint in the Magistrate Court where the parent resides. The court may issue summons to the child's last known Bangladeshi address or coordinate notice, and the NRB child can appear through an authorised advocate.
